# ARGs with `line` `dependence-and-domination`

*Lines of inquiry — A named line of the record's own argument, so that a line can be set aside as a whole and what depends on it can be found. Retracting a line is a status change on its members, never a deletion (ADR-032).*

**Wholes, parts and dependence** — what wholes and their parts owe and can claim of each other, and when a dependence becomes domination or exploitation — control over the terms on which a dependence is met, not the size of the dependence, decides which way it runs and whether a whole's need of a part is the part's hold; exploitation and domination are judged against a standard declared with the judgment; and those who control an arrangement others depend on owe accountability and justification that rise with how indispensable it has become and how durably their choices narrow what is later open. "Organization" here is TERM-074's sense 1, a relational arrangement, unless an entry says otherwise, and the bearers of obligations, agents or roles, are kept apart from the ground of the obligation; split from organizational-normativity (ADR-100).

| [ARG-117](../../../record/arguments.d/ARG-117.md) | Locke's Second Treatise carries the form of the claim that no delegation can confer what the delegator lacks, but grounds it in the absence of power over one's own life and admits forfeiture by fault, so it does not carry inalienable standing in general | The support judgement the readings of 2026-11-18 make about [CLAIM-720](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-720.md), filed "after Locke's Second Treatise §§22–23 and 135". Skimmed on the cited sections ([NOTE-2077](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2077.md)), Locke carries the form: "No body can give more power than he has himself" (§23), and "no body has an absolute arbitrary power over himself" (§135). He does not carry the claim's generality. His ground is that persons are God's "property, whose workmanship they are" (§6), so what cannot be conferred is arbitrary power over life. And he admits forfeiture: one "having by his fault forfeited his own life" (§23). The claim lists no wrongdoing among what cannot remove standing, and its defeat condition does not address forfeiture.
